gloss: Something bad that happens by chance and hurts someone or damages something.
examples: There was an *accident* on the highway this morning.
Most home *accidents* happen in the kitchen.
He broke his wrist in a bike *accident*.

gloss: A door kept clear so people can leave a building or vehicle quickly in danger.
examples: The *emergency exit* is at the back of the store.
Please locate the two nearest *emergency exits*.
Never block an *emergency exit* with boxes.

gloss: A device or signal that warns everyone in a building that there is a fire.
examples: Somebody pulled the *fire alarm* during third period.
The *fire alarm* went off at two in the morning.
All the *fire alarms* are tested twice a year.

gloss: A metal cylinder of chemicals or foam used to put out a small fire.
examples: Keep a *fire extinguisher* under the kitchen sink.
He grabbed the *fire extinguisher* and aimed it at the base of the flames.
The *fire extinguishers* in the hallway were all expired.

gloss: A small ceiling device that senses smoke and sounds a loud warning.
examples: The *smoke detector* goes off every time I make toast.
Change the battery in your *smoke detector* twice a year.
The landlord installed *smoke detectors* in every bedroom.

gloss: A device that makes a loud sound when it senses smoke in a room.
examples: Our *smoke alarm* started chirping at midnight.
A working *smoke alarm* doubles your chance of getting out alive.
The fire department gives away free *smoke alarms*.
contrast: Americans use *smoke alarm* and *smoke detector* for the same ceiling unit.

gloss: A practice in which everyone leaves a building as if there were a fire.
examples: We had a *fire drill* right before lunch.
The school runs a *fire drill* every month.
Nobody takes *fire drills* seriously until there's a real fire.

gloss: A lighted sign that shows the way out of a building.
examples: Follow the green *exit sign* down the stairs.
The *exit sign* over the door was burned out.
*Exit signs* have to stay lit even in a power failure.
contrast: *Exit* is said either /ˈɛɡzɪt/ or /ˈɛksɪt/ — both are normal American.

gloss: The act of getting away from a dangerous place or situation.
examples: Their *escape* from the burning building was captured on video.
It was a narrow *escape* — the roof fell in a minute later.
Both *escapes* happened through a basement window.

gloss: The path people are meant to follow to get out of danger.
examples: Plan an *escape route* from every room in the house.
The smoke cut off their only *escape route*.
*Escape routes* are marked on the back of the hotel door.

gloss: An act of saving someone from danger.
examples: The *rescue* took six hours in freezing water.
Divers came to the *rescue* of the trapped crew.
The crew has made more than forty *rescues* this year.

gloss: A person who saves someone from danger.
examples: Her *rescuer* was a neighbor with a ladder.
*Rescuers* dug through the snow for two days.
The *rescuers* reached the hikers just before dark.

gloss: A police officer, firefighter, or medical worker who is first to arrive at an emergency.
examples: The *first responder* on the scene was a volunteer firefighter.
*First responders* pulled two people from the car.
The town held a breakfast to thank its *first responders*.

gloss: The part of a hospital that treats people who need help immediately.
examples: We spent five hours in the *emergency room*.
Take him to the *emergency room* if the bleeding doesn't stop.
Rural *emergency rooms* are closing all over the state.
contrast: Americans shorten this to *the ER*; the British say *A&E*.

gloss: A box or bag of supplies for treating small injuries.
examples: There's a *first aid kit* in the trunk of the car.
The *first aid kit* was missing its bandages.
Every classroom keeps two *first aid kits*.

gloss: Something said or shown to tell people that danger is coming.
examples: The storm hit without any *warning*.
He ignored the *warnings* and swam out anyway.
The weather service issued a *warning* for three counties.

gloss: A sign that tells people about a danger ahead.
examples: A yellow *warning sign* marks the drop-off.
Somebody had knocked over the *warning sign*.
*Warning signs* were posted all along the fence.

gloss: Printed text on a product that tells you how it can hurt you.
examples: Read the *warning label* before you use the cleaner.
The bottle carries a *warning label* about fumes.
*Warning labels* on ladders are there for a reason.

gloss: Care taken to avoid danger or mistakes.
examples: Handle the gas can with *caution*.
Drivers should use extra *caution* on wet roads.
A little *caution* would have prevented the whole thing.

gloss: Something you do in advance to keep harm from happening.
examples: Wearing a helmet is a simple *precaution*.
They took every *precaution* before the storm.
The usual *precautions* weren't enough this time.

gloss: The state of being kept safe from harm, or the means of keeping something safe.
examples: These gloves offer good *protection* against cuts.
The wall gave them *protection* from the wind.
Sunscreen is your best *protection* on the water.

gloss: The work of stopping something bad before it happens.
examples: The talk was about fire *prevention* in older homes.
*Prevention* is cheaper than a rescue.
Accident *prevention* is part of every shift meeting.

gloss: A person who stays alive through an accident or disaster.
examples: The only *survivor* was a boy in the back seat.
Crews searched the rubble for *survivors*.
*Survivors* were taken to a shelter downtown.

gloss: The fact of staying alive, especially in dangerous conditions.
examples: *Survival* in that water is measured in minutes.
The class covers cold-weather *survival*.
Their *survival* came down to one dry blanket.

gloss: A sudden event that causes great damage or loss of life.
examples: The flood was the worst *disaster* in the county's history.
Natural *disasters* cost the state billions last year.
The governor declared the fire a *disaster*.

gloss: A disaster of the very worst kind.
examples: A leak that size could turn into a *catastrophe*.
The dam failure was an avoidable *catastrophe*.
Two *catastrophes* in one summer emptied the relief fund.
contrast: The final *-e* is pronounced: kuh-TAS-truh-fee, with the stress on the second syllable.

gloss: A crash in which two moving things hit each other.
examples: The *collision* happened at the intersection.
Nobody was hurt in the *collision*.
Head-on *collisions* are the deadliest kind.

gloss: An event, usually an unpleasant one, that has to be reported or dealt with.
examples: The *incident* was over before the police arrived.
File a report after any *incident* on the job site.
There have been three *incidents* at that crossing this year.

gloss: A small accident that causes trouble but little harm.
examples: We got there after a couple of *mishaps* with the trailer.
A kitchen *mishap* set off the smoke alarm.
The trip went fine except for one *mishap* on the ice.

gloss: A crash in which many vehicles run into one another.
examples: Fog caused a twenty-car *pileup* on the interstate.
The *pileup* closed both lanes until evening.
Winter *pileups* are common on that stretch.
contrast: One word as a noun (*a pileup*), two as a verb (*cars piled up*).

gloss: A minor car crash that damages the body of the car but hurts nobody.
examples: It was just a *fender bender* in the parking lot.
Her first *fender bender* raised the insurance rate.
Two *fender benders* on the same corner in one week.
contrast: American and informal; the British would say *a bump* or *a prang*.

gloss: The place where a plane, train, or vehicle came down or wrecked.
examples: Investigators spent a week at the *crash site*.
The *crash site* is still closed to the public.
Both *crash sites* were deep in the woods.

gloss: A landing a pilot has to make right away because something has gone wrong.
examples: The plane made an *emergency landing* in a cornfield.
Smoke in the cabin forced an *emergency landing*.
The airport handles a few *emergency landings* a year.

gloss: The sudden falling down of a building, roof, or other structure.
examples: The *collapse* trapped four workers in the basement.
Heavy snow caused the roof *collapse*.
Two *collapses* in one week shut down the mine.

gloss: A violent explosion, or the rush of air it sends out.
examples: The *blast* blew out windows two blocks away.
She was knocked down by the *blast*.
Neighbors heard two *blasts* before the fire started.

gloss: Broken pieces left after something is destroyed.
examples: The road was covered with *debris* after the storm.
Crews cleared the *debris* by hand.
Flying *debris* is what hurts most people in a tornado.
contrast: The final *s* is silent, and Americans stress the second syllable: duh-BREE.

gloss: What is left of a vehicle or building that has been destroyed.
examples: They pulled the driver from the *wreckage*.
The *wreckage* is still on the shoulder of the road.
Divers found *wreckage* about a mile offshore.
contrast: The *w* is silent, as in *wreck* and *wrist*.

gloss: Very great damage over a wide area.
examples: The *devastation* along the coast was hard to look at.
Nothing prepared them for the *devastation*.
Photos showed block after block of *devastation*.

gloss: The work of clearing away damage, waste, or a spill.
examples: The *cleanup* after the flood took months.
Volunteers showed up for the *cleanup* on Saturday.
Chemical *cleanups* are expensive and slow.
contrast: One word as a noun (*the cleanup*), two as a verb (*they clean up*).

gloss: A death caused by an accident, disaster, or violence.
examples: There was one *fatality* in the crash.
The fire caused no *fatalities*.
Traffic *fatalities* dropped again last year.

gloss: The number of people killed by a disaster or accident.
examples: The *death toll* rose to nineteen overnight.
Officials expect the *death toll* to climb.
*Death tolls* from these storms are usually low.

gloss: A person who has been moved away from a dangerous area.
examples: The high school gym is full of *evacuees*.
Each *evacuee* got a cot and a hot meal.
*Evacuees* were allowed home on Thursday.

gloss: An official instruction telling people they must leave an area.
examples: The county issued an *evacuation order* at noon.
They stayed even after the *evacuation order* came.
*Evacuation orders* were lifted for two neighborhoods.

gloss: An official declaration that lets a government act quickly in a crisis.
examples: The governor declared a *state of emergency* before the storm.
A *state of emergency* frees up federal money.
Three *states of emergency* were declared that summer.
contrast: The plural adds *-s* to the first word: *states of emergency*.

gloss: A period when people must stay inside a building or area for safety.
examples: The school went into *lockdown* for an hour.
The *lockdown* ended once police cleared the building.
Two *lockdowns* in one semester rattled the parents.
contrast: One word as a noun (*a lockdown*), two as a verb (*they lock down the building*).

gloss: Shelter or safety from danger or bad weather.
examples: They took *refuge* in the basement.
The church offered *refuge* to families who lost their homes.
Hikers found *refuge* from the storm in an old cabin.

gloss: A strong underground or reinforced room where people wait out a tornado or hurricane.
examples: Every house on the block has a *storm shelter*.
We spent an hour in the *storm shelter*.
The town built two public *storm shelters*.

gloss: A bag of sand stacked to hold back water or stop bullets.
examples: He filled another *sandbag* and passed it down the line.
*Sandbags* kept the water out of the shop.
The city handed out free *sandbags* all weekend.

gloss: The wall of seawater a hurricane pushes onto the shore.
examples: The *storm surge* reached eight feet.
Most of the damage came from the *storm surge*, not the wind.
*Storm surges* flood the same streets every time.

gloss: A smaller earthquake that follows a larger one.
examples: An *aftershock* woke everybody at four in the morning.
There were dozens of *aftershocks* that week.
Rescue work stopped during each *aftershock*.

gloss: A small shaking of the ground.
examples: A *tremor* rattled the windows.
Residents felt two *tremors* before dawn.
The *tremor* lasted only a few seconds.

gloss: The sudden start of something dangerous, such as disease or fires.
examples: The *outbreak* began at a summer camp.
An *outbreak* of wildfires closed the highway.
Health officials tracked three separate *outbreaks*.

gloss: A sudden rush of frightened people or animals in one direction.
examples: The false alarm set off a *stampede* toward the doors.
Several people were hurt in the *stampede*.
Crowd barriers are meant to prevent *stampedes*.

gloss: Serious danger, especially danger to life.
examples: The crew was in real *peril* by midnight.
He ignored the sign at his own *peril*.
The film shows the *perils* of climbing alone.

gloss: Something that makes a fire likely to start or spread.
examples: That pile of oily rags is a *fire hazard*.
The inspector listed six *fire hazards* in the kitchen.
Space heaters are a common *fire hazard*.

gloss: A small object a child could swallow and choke on.
examples: The box says the toy is a *choking hazard* for kids under three.
Grapes are a *choking hazard* unless you cut them.
We removed all the *choking hazards* from the playroom.

gloss: An escape of gas from a pipe or tank, which can poison people or explode.
examples: The building was evacuated because of a *gas leak*.
If you smell a *gas leak*, get outside and call from the street.
Crews found two small *gas leaks* under the sidewalk.

gloss: Strong, often harmful gas or smoke given off by chemicals, fuel, or burning.
examples: Open a window — the paint *fumes* are terrible.
He passed out from exhaust *fumes* in the garage.
The *fumes* set off the alarm on the second floor.
contrast: Always plural in form: *the fumes were strong*, never *a fume*.

gloss: A poisonous substance, especially one made by a living thing.
examples: The smoke carries a *toxin* that damages the lungs.
Tests found several *toxins* in the well water.
The *toxin* takes hours to show any effect.

gloss: The presence of something dirty, poisonous, or infectious where it does not belong.
examples: The plant was closed after *contamination* was found.
*Contamination* of the water supply is the main worry.
They took soil samples to check for *contamination*.

gloss: A living thing or biological waste that can spread disease.
examples: Used needles go in the *biohazard* container.
The room was sealed off as a *biohazard*.
Hospitals label these bags as *biohazards*.

gloss: A poisonous gas with no smell, made when fuel burns without enough air.
examples: *Carbon monoxide* killed the family in their sleep.
Never run a generator indoors — it gives off *carbon monoxide*.
The furnace was leaking *carbon monoxide*.

gloss: A device that sounds an alarm when carbon monoxide builds up in a room.
examples: State law requires a *carbon monoxide detector* near every bedroom.
The *carbon monoxide detector* went off at three in the morning.
We put *carbon monoxide detectors* on both floors.

gloss: Illness or death caused by a poisonous substance getting into the body.
examples: Two workers were treated for *poisoning*.
Lead *poisoning* is still a problem in old houses.
Call a doctor if you suspect *poisoning*.

gloss: A medicine that works against a particular poison.
examples: There is an *antidote* for that snake's venom.
The hospital keeps the *antidote* on hand.
Some poisons have no *antidotes* at all.

gloss: The flow of blood from a wound.
examples: Press on the cut to stop the *bleeding*.
The *bleeding* slowed once they raised his arm.
Heavy *bleeding* needs a doctor, not a bandage.

gloss: Death caused by being under water and unable to breathe.
examples: *Drowning* is silent — nobody hears it happen.
There were four *drownings* on the lake last summer.
Most *drownings* happen within sight of help.

gloss: A dangerous drop in body temperature from cold.
examples: The hikers were treated for *hypothermia*.
*Hypothermia* can set in even at fifty degrees if you're wet.
Shivering is the first sign of *hypothermia*.

gloss: Weakness, dizziness, and heavy sweating caused by working in heat.
examples: Two roofers went home with *heat exhaustion*.
*Heat exhaustion* turns into heatstroke if you ignore it.
Cold water and shade will usually fix *heat exhaustion*.
contrast: *Exhaustion* begins with the sound /ɪɡz/, not /ɛks/: ig-ZAWS-chun.

gloss: Death or serious injury caused by electric current passing through the body.
examples: Downed wires are a real risk of *electrocution*.
The report blamed *electrocution* for both deaths.
Rubber-soled boots reduce the danger of *electrocution*.

gloss: A burn caused by very hot liquid or steam.
examples: The coffee left a nasty *scald* on her wrist.
Most kitchen *scalds* happen to small children.
Run cool water over a *scald* for ten minutes.

gloss: Damage to the lungs from breathing smoke during a fire.
examples: Three residents were treated for *smoke inhalation*.
*Smoke inhalation* kills more people in fires than flames do.
He was hospitalized overnight with *smoke inhalation*.

gloss: Chest presses and rescue breaths used to keep blood moving in someone whose heart has stopped.
examples: A bystander started *CPR* right there on the sidewalk.
Every lifeguard is trained in *CPR*.
She kept doing *CPR* until the ambulance came.
contrast: Said as three letters; the full form *cardiopulmonary resuscitation* is almost never spoken.

gloss: The act of bringing someone back to consciousness or breathing.
examples: *Resuscitation* went on for twenty minutes.
The team's attempts at *resuscitation* worked.
He signed a form refusing *resuscitation*.
contrast: The *sc* is just an /s/ sound: rih-SUS-uh-TAY-shun.

gloss: The sorting of injured people so the most urgent cases are treated first.
examples: Nurses set up *triage* in the parking lot.
*Triage* decided who went into the first ambulance.
He spent the night doing *triage* after the crash.

gloss: A person trained to give medical help at the scene of an emergency.
examples: A *medic* checked her breathing at the curb.
*Medics* were on the field within seconds.
The *medic* said it was only a sprain.

gloss: A trained worker who gives emergency care and rides in an ambulance.
examples: The *EMT* put a collar on his neck before moving him.
Two *EMTs* lifted her onto the stretcher.
She works nights as an *EMT*.
contrast: Said as three letters and written *EMT* — short for *emergency medical technician*.

gloss: The person who takes emergency calls and sends out police, fire, or ambulance crews.
examples: The *dispatcher* stayed on the line with her.
*Dispatchers* handled forty calls in an hour.
Tell the *dispatcher* your exact address first.

gloss: A machine that shocks a stopped heart back into rhythm.
examples: There's a *defibrillator* on the wall by the elevator.
The coach used the *defibrillator* before help arrived.
The gym keeps two *defibrillators* on site.

gloss: A tight band put around an arm or leg to stop heavy bleeding.
examples: He tied a *tourniquet* above the wound.
The kit holds gauze, tape, and a *tourniquet*.
*Tourniquets* saved a lot of lives in that crash.
contrast: The French spelling hides an ordinary ending: TUR-nih-kit, not "-kay".

gloss: A stiff piece of material tied to a broken limb to keep it still.
examples: They made a *splint* out of a rolled magazine.
The nurse put a *splint* on his finger.
Both *splints* came off after three weeks.

gloss: A cloth loop worn around the neck to support an injured arm.
examples: She had her arm in a *sling* for a month.
The *sling* keeps the shoulder from moving.
The clinic gave out *slings* and ice packs.

gloss: A wheeled bed used to move patients in a hospital or ambulance.
examples: They wheeled him out on a *gurney*.
The *gurney* wouldn't fit through the doorway.
Two *gurneys* were parked in the hallway.
contrast: An American word; the British say *trolley*.

gloss: A cold pad held against an injury to cut swelling and pain.
examples: Put an *ice pack* on that ankle.
The *ice pack* melted in twenty minutes.
There are *ice packs* in the freezer at work.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A liquid or cream put on a cut to kill germs.
examples: Clean the scrape and put some *antiseptic* on it.
The kit has an *antiseptic* and a roll of tape.
Hospital *antiseptics* are stronger than the drugstore kind.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A chemical used to kill germs on surfaces and equipment.
examples: Wipe the counter down with *disinfectant*.
They ran out of *disinfectant* by Tuesday.
Strong *disinfectants* can irritate your lungs.

gloss: A hospital equipped to treat the most serious injuries.
examples: He was flown to the nearest *trauma center*.
The *trauma center* is an hour away by road.
There are only three *trauma centers* in the state.

gloss: Any vehicle used by police, firefighters, or medical crews to answer calls.
examples: Pull over when an *emergency vehicle* comes up behind you.
The *emergency vehicle* had its lights on but no siren.
Three *emergency vehicles* blocked the intersection.
contrast: The *h* in *vehicle* is silent: VEE-uh-kuhl.

gloss: The moving of people or supplies by aircraft when roads cannot be used.
examples: The *airlift* brought food to the cut-off town.
An *airlift* took the injured climber to the hospital.
Two *airlifts* went out before the weather closed in.

gloss: A team trained and equipped to reach and save people in danger.
examples: The *rescue squad* got there in eight minutes.
Our town's *rescue squad* is all volunteers.
Two *rescue squads* worked the river together.

gloss: The work of finding and saving people who are lost or trapped.
examples: *Search and rescue* began at first light.
He flies helicopters for *search and rescue*.
The county pays for *search and rescue* out of its own budget.

gloss: A group of people who go out together to look for someone missing.
examples: A *search party* set out along the ridge.
Neighbors formed a *search party* before dawn.
Two *search parties* covered opposite sides of the lake.

gloss: A trained dog that finds people buried or lost.
examples: A *rescue dog* found the boy under the porch.
*Rescue dogs* worked the rubble in shifts.
The *rescue dog* wears boots on hot pavement.
contrast: In everyday talk a *rescue dog* can also mean a dog adopted from a shelter.

gloss: A police team that handles and removes explosives.
examples: The *bomb squad* closed the block for two hours.
A *bomb squad* robot opened the suitcase.
*Bomb squads* from two cities responded.
contrast: The *b* at the end of *bomb* is silent: BAHM.

gloss: A set of straps worn around the body and clipped to a rope to stop a fall.
examples: Nobody goes on the roof without a *harness*.
His *harness* caught him halfway down.
The crew checks the *harnesses* every morning.

gloss: A net stretched below people working or performing high up.
examples: The acrobats work above a *safety net*.
A *safety net* hung under the bridge deck.
*Safety nets* are required on any job over thirty feet.

gloss: A bar along stairs or a walkway that you hold for support.
examples: Hold the *handrail* — those steps are icy.
The *handrail* came loose from the wall.
They added *handrails* on both sides of the ramp.

gloss: A fence, wall, or bar that keeps people out of a dangerous place.
examples: A concrete *barrier* separates the lanes.
Police put up a *barrier* around the sinkhole.
The crowd pushed against the *barriers*.

gloss: A quickly built wall or fence set up to block a street or doorway.
examples: Crews set up a *barricade* at the end of the block.
Someone moved the *barricade* and drove through.
Wooden *barricades* lined the parade route.

gloss: An orange plastic cone used to mark off a hazard or closed lane.
examples: A *traffic cone* marked the open manhole.
Somebody knocked over half the *traffic cones*.
The crew set *traffic cones* every twenty feet.

gloss: Bright yellow plastic ribbon strung around a dangerous or restricted area.
examples: They ran *caution tape* across the driveway.
Don't step past the *caution tape*.
There was *caution tape* around the whole block.

gloss: A barrier across a road that stops or turns back traffic.
examples: There's a *roadblock* at the bottom of the hill.
Police set up a *roadblock* on the bridge.
*Roadblocks* kept everyone out of the burn area.

gloss: A raised strip across a road that forces drivers to slow down.
examples: Take the *speed bump* slowly or you'll scrape the bumper.
The school asked the city for a *speed bump*.
There are four *speed bumps* in the parking lot.

gloss: The separate brake that holds a parked car or stops it if the main brakes fail.
examples: Set the *emergency brake* on that hill.
The *emergency brake* was frozen solid.
*Emergency brakes* rust if you never use them.
contrast: *Brake* sounds exactly like *break*; the British call this the *handbrake*.

gloss: A mask with filters that keeps dust, fumes, or germs out of the lungs.
examples: Wear a *respirator* when you sand that paint.
His *respirator* fogged up in the heat.
The shop keeps *respirators* by the door.

gloss: A light paper mask that keeps dust out of your nose and mouth.
examples: Grab a *dust mask* before you go in the attic.
A *dust mask* won't protect you from fumes.
*Dust masks* come ten to a box.

gloss: A mask covering the whole face that filters out poisonous gas.
examples: The crew went in wearing *gas masks*.
His *gas mask* was fitted the week before.
A *gas mask* is useless without the right filter.

gloss: A clear plastic guard worn over the whole face.
examples: Put a *face shield* on before you start grinding.
The *face shield* took the spark instead of his eye.
*Face shields* hang next to the goggles.

gloss: Tough clear glasses worn to keep chips and dust out of the eyes.
examples: You need *safety glasses* to run that saw.
My *safety glasses* are scratched up.
The shop hands out three pairs of *safety glasses* a year.
contrast: Plural only — count them in pairs: *a pair of safety glasses*.

gloss: A bright orange or yellow vest that makes a worker easy to see.
examples: Everybody on the site wears a *safety vest*.
Her *safety vest* was hanging on the truck mirror.
The crossing guards got new *safety vests*.

gloss: The clothing and equipment worn to keep a worker from being hurt.
examples: Firefighters carry sixty pounds of *protective gear*.
All of the *protective gear* is stored in that locker.
You can't enter the lab without *protective gear*.
contrast: Uncountable in English: *a lot of protective gear*, never *a protective gear*.

gloss: A sealed full-body suit worn around dangerous chemicals or germs.
examples: Two workers in *hazmat suits* went into the tank room.
The *hazmat suit* gets unbearably hot in ten minutes.
They keep four *hazmat suits* on the truck.
contrast: *Hazmat* is short for *hazardous materials*.

gloss: An inflatable boat carried on a ship or plane for use if it sinks or ditches.
examples: The crew climbed into the *life raft*.
The *life raft* inflates as soon as it hits the water.
Both *life rafts* were found empty.

gloss: A ring or vest that keeps a person floating in the water.
examples: He threw her a *life preserver* from the dock.
There's a *life preserver* on each side of the boat.
The *life preservers* were locked in a cabinet.
contrast: American; the British say *lifebelt* or *lifebuoy*.

gloss: Anything designed to keep a person afloat in water.
examples: Your seat cushion can be used as a *flotation device*.
Children must wear a *flotation device* on the dock.
The store sells *flotation devices* for toddlers.

gloss: A rope thrown or fixed to keep someone from being lost or swept away.
examples: He tied a *lifeline* around his waist before going out on the ice.
A *lifeline* runs the length of the deck.
The radio was their only *lifeline*.

gloss: A narrow flow of water that pulls swimmers away from the beach.
examples: A *rip current* carried him out past the sandbar.
Swim sideways to get out of a *rip current*.
*Rip currents* kill more swimmers here than sharks do.

gloss: The state of being in serious trouble and needing help.
examples: The boat was in *distress* about two miles out.
They picked up a *distress* call at midnight.
The plane signaled *distress* and turned back.

gloss: The spoken radio call used by a ship or aircraft in serious danger.
examples: The pilot put out a *mayday* over the water.
The tower recorded the *mayday* at 4:12.
Two *maydays* came in during the storm.
contrast: From French *m'aidez* ("help me") — nothing to do with the holiday May Day.

gloss: A bright burning light fired or lit to signal for help or mark a hazard.
examples: He set a *flare* behind the stalled truck.
A *flare* went up from the far side of the lake.
Keep road *flares* in the trunk all winter.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *flair*, which means a natural talent.

gloss: A wide-barreled pistol that fires a signal flare into the sky.
examples: The boat carries a *flare gun* and three shells.
She fired the *flare gun* straight up.
*Flare guns* are checked with the rest of the safety kit.

gloss: A light or radio signal that guides rescuers or warns of danger.
examples: The plane's emergency *beacon* led searchers to the wreck.
A *beacon* flashes on top of the tower.
Climbers carry avalanche *beacons*.

gloss: A powerful lamp whose beam can be aimed to look for something in the dark.
examples: The helicopter's *searchlight* swept the field.
A *searchlight* found the boat near the rocks.
Two *searchlights* lit up the riverbank.

gloss: A cone-shaped device that makes a voice loud enough for a crowd to hear.
examples: An officer gave directions through a *megaphone*.
The *megaphone* batteries died halfway through.
They handed out *megaphones* to the block captains.

gloss: An electric megaphone used to shout instructions to a crowd.
examples: The fire chief shouted through a *bullhorn*.
Someone raised a *bullhorn* and told everyone to move back.
The police brought two *bullhorns*.
contrast: American for *megaphone*; the British stick with *megaphone* or *loudhailer*.

gloss: A small two-way radio you carry in your hand.
examples: Keep the *walkie-talkie* on channel three.
His *walkie-talkie* crackled and went dead.
The crew works with *walkie-talkies* inside the building.

gloss: A phone line set up so people can get help or report a problem quickly.
examples: The county set up a *hotline* for storm damage.
She called the poison *hotline* at two in the morning.
Both *hotlines* were busy all night.

gloss: A button pressed to call for help immediately.
examples: The teller hit the *panic button* under the counter.
Every room has a *panic button* by the bed.
The new alarm came with two *panic buttons*.

gloss: A warning of danger that turns out to be wrong.
examples: It was only a *false alarm* — burned popcorn.
The department answers hundreds of *false alarms* a year.
After the third *false alarm*, nobody moved.

gloss: The person a school or employer calls if something happens to you.
examples: Put your sister down as your *emergency contact*.
They couldn't reach his *emergency contact*.
The form asks for two *emergency contacts*.

gloss: A packed set of supplies for staying alive until help arrives.
examples: Keep a *survival kit* in the car during winter.
The *survival kit* has water, a blanket, and matches.
They sell *survival kits* at the hardware store.

gloss: A person paid to watch a building or area and keep it safe.
examples: The *security guard* walked us to our car.
A *security guard* found the broken window.
Two *security guards* work the night shift.

gloss: A camera that records what happens in a building or on a street.
examples: A *security camera* caught the whole thing.
The *security camera* over the door isn't working.
There are *security cameras* in every hallway.

gloss: A light that comes on to show something is wrong or dangerous.
examples: A red *warning light* came on over the door.
Don't ignore that *warning light* on the dash.
All the *warning lights* flashed at once.

gloss: The rules and habits that keep fires from starting or spreading.
examples: The class covers *fire safety* in the home.
*Fire safety* starts with a clear exit path.
He teaches *fire safety* at the elementary school.

gloss: The work of putting out fires.
examples: *Firefighting* is harder than it looks on television.
He spent thirty years in *firefighting*.
The town spends most of its budget on *firefighting*.

gloss: A truck carrying a pump, hoses, and water to a fire.
examples: Three *fire engines* pulled up outside.
The *fire engine* couldn't get down the narrow street.
Kids waved at the *fire engine* in the parade.
contrast: Americans say both *fire engine* and *fire truck* for the same vehicle.

gloss: The building where firefighters and their trucks are based.
examples: The *firehouse* on Third Street has been there a century.
They hold a pancake breakfast at the *firehouse*.
Both *firehouses* closed in the budget cuts.
contrast: A homey American word for *fire station*.

gloss: A man whose job is putting out fires.
examples: A *fireman* carried the cat down the ladder.
Two *firemen* stayed behind to watch the embers.
My grandfather was a *fireman* for twenty years.
contrast: Irregular plural *firemen*; the neutral modern word is *firefighter*.

gloss: The officer in charge of a fire department.
examples: The *fire chief* spoke to reporters at the scene.
Our *fire chief* has been on the job since 1998.
Two former *fire chiefs* came to the ceremony.

gloss: An official who inspects buildings and investigates the causes of fires.
examples: The *fire marshal* closed the club for overcrowding.
A *fire marshal* is still looking into the cause.
*Fire marshals* check every school in the county.
contrast: *Marshal* sounds just like *martial*, and American spelling keeps only one *l*.

gloss: The heavy hose that carries water from a hydrant or truck to a fire.
examples: It takes two people to hold a *fire hose*.
The *fire hose* was still charged with water.
*Fire hoses* ran across the whole intersection.

gloss: A heavy door that holds back flames and smoke for a set time.
examples: Never prop open a *fire door*.
The *fire door* kept the smoke out of the stairwell.
All the *fire doors* close automatically when the alarm sounds.

gloss: A sheet of fireproof cloth thrown over flames to smother them.
examples: She smothered the grease fire with a *fire blanket*.
A *fire blanket* hangs by the stove.
The lab keeps *fire blankets* at both exits.

gloss: A folding ladder kept upstairs to climb out a window in a fire.
examples: There's an *escape ladder* under the bed.
The *escape ladder* hooks over the window sill.
We bought *escape ladders* for both bedrooms.

gloss: A large, bright fire.
examples: Crews fought the *blaze* for six hours.
The *blaze* started in a back room.
Two *blazes* broke out the same night.

gloss: A huge fire that is out of control.
examples: The warehouse became an *inferno* in minutes.
Firefighters could only watch the *inferno* from the street.
Summer *infernos* like this used to be rare.

gloss: A small piece of burning or glowing material left from a fire.
examples: An *ember* landed on the roof next door.
Wind carried *embers* half a mile.
He soaked the *embers* before going to bed.

gloss: A person who sets fire to property on purpose.
examples: Investigators think an *arsonist* started it.
The *arsonist* used gasoline and a rag.
Two *arsonists* were arrested that fall.
